program_overview.title: Ontario Computer Science Companion: ICS3U and ICS4U
program_overview.tagline: A second teacher for Grade 11 and Grade 12 computer science: problem solving first, then clean code in Python or Java, in step with your school course.
program_overview.description:
ICS3U (Introduction to Computer Science, Grade 11, University Preparation) and ICS4U (Computer Science, Grade 12, University Preparation) are Ontario's university-preparation computer science courses, described in the ministry's Computer Studies curriculum for Grades 10 to 12 (2008). The ministry describes ICS3U this way: "Students will design software independently and as part of a team, using industry-standard programming tools and applying the software development life-cycle model". For ICS4U it says: "Students will use modular design principles to create complex and fully documented programs, according to industry standards". In each Grade 11 and 12 course, the curriculum document says, the first strand is Programming Concepts and Skills and the second is Software Development, and the fourth strand "deals with the role of computers in society". ICS3U has no prerequisite; ICS4U requires "Introduction to Computer Science, Grade 11, University Preparation", which is ICS3U.

This course runs alongside the student's own ICS3U or ICS4U class. We teach in whichever language the school uses, Python or Java, and we follow the order of the student's school course outline, so what is learned here is used in class the same week. Every topic starts with the problem before the syntax: reading the task, breaking it into steps, writing the algorithm in plain words, then turning it into code and testing it. From there we build data types, control structures, lists and arrays, modular programming with functions or methods, string and file handling, sorting and searching, and for ICS4U students, recursion and object-oriented design. Assignments and the final project or exam are the student's own work: we explain, question and review, and the student writes the code.

Please read this plainly: Modern Age Coders teaches alongside school and does not grant Ontario high school credits. ICS3U and ICS4U are each worth one credit, and families who need the credit take the course through their school or a ministry-inspected credit provider. What we add is understanding, practice and confidence, in live classes with a real teacher.

phase_1_problem_solving_and_ics3u_core.title: PHASE 1: Problem Solving and the ICS3U Core (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_problem_solving_and_ics3u_core.description: How a programmer thinks before typing, then the building blocks every ICS3U program uses, in Python or Java.

month_1_algorithms_and_data.title: Month 1: Algorithms, Data Types and Input and Output

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Problem Solving Before Syntax
topics: A starting conversation and short diagnostic: the school, the language, the course outline and the next assignment
Reading a programming task and listing the inputs, outputs and rules
Writing an algorithm as numbered plain-word steps, then as pseudocode
Flowcharts for decisions and repetition, kept simple
Tracing an algorithm by hand with a trace table
Setting up the school's editor or IDE at home so practice matches class
projects: Three small problems solved twice: once as plain-word steps, once as working code
week_1_2.practice: Write the algorithm for each practice task before opening the editor, and keep both

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Data Types, Variables and Expressions
topics: Integers, decimals, text and true or false values, in Python and in Java
Static types in Java and dynamic types in Python, and what each means for errors
Arithmetic, integer division and remainder, and the rounding surprises they cause
Reading input and converting it to the right type
Formatting output neatly, as school assignments usually require
Naming variables so a marker can follow the code
projects: A unit converter or bill splitter with clear prompts, checked input and formatted output
week_3_4.practice: Short daily tracing questions: predict the output, then run the code to check
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a short written trace plus one small program, reviewed with written feedback

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Decisions
topics: if, else if and else in Python and Java
Boolean expressions with and, or and not
Nested decisions and when to flatten them
Testing every branch: choosing test cases on purpose
Validating input so a program does not crash on a bad value
Comparing text correctly, including the Java equals trap
projects: A rules-based program, such as a ticket pricing or grading-rules calculator, with a written test plan
week_5_6.practice: For every decision program, list the test cases first and record the expected results

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Loops
topics: Counted loops and condition-controlled loops
Running totals, counters and finding the largest or smallest value
Loops that validate input until it is correct
Nested loops for tables and patterns
Off-by-one errors and how a trace table catches them
Choosing a for loop or a while loop for the job
projects: A number guessing game or a times-table quiz with scoring and replay
week_7_8.practice: A loop tracing set: write the value of every variable after each pass
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a written tracing section and a short program, marked with comments

phase_2_completing_ics3u.title: PHASE 2: Completing ICS3U (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_completing_ics3u.description: The data structures, modular design, files and classic algorithms that larger ICS3U programs need, plus the software development habits the course describes.

month_3_lists_and_modular_programming.title: Month 3: Lists, Arrays and Modular Programming

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Lists and Arrays
topics: Python lists, Java arrays and Java ArrayList, and how they differ
Looping through a collection by index and by value
Parallel lists and when a better structure is needed
Searching a list for a value, counting matches and filtering
Two-dimensional lists and arrays for grids and tables
Index errors: why they happen and how to prevent them
projects: A class marks analyzer: store scores, report the average, the highest and lowest, and a simple bar display
week_9_10.practice: Short list and array tasks, each with a trace of the indexes visited

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Modular Programming with Functions and Methods
topics: Breaking a program into functions in Python or static methods in Java
Parameters, return values and why a function should do one job
Local and global scope, and avoiding hidden shared state
Writing a short comment or docstring that says what a function does
Testing one function at a time
Refactoring a long program into clear modules
projects: Refactor an earlier project into well-named functions or methods, with a test for each
week_11_12.practice: For each new function, write its purpose, its inputs and its output before the body
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a modular program built from a given plan, reviewed for structure and clarity

month_4_strings_files_sorting_searching.title: Month 4: Strings, Files, Sorting and Searching

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: String and File Handling
topics: Strings as sequences: indexing, slicing or substring, and length
Common string tasks: counting letters, reversing, checking palindromes, simple ciphers
Splitting a line of text into fields and joining fields back together
Reading a text file line by line in Python and in Java
Writing results to a file and handling a missing file safely
Processing a small data file from start to finish
projects: A file report tool: read a data file, summarize it and write a tidy results file
week_13_14.practice: String puzzles and short file tasks, with the expected output written before running

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Sorting, Searching and the Development Life Cycle
topics: Linear search and binary search, and when binary search is allowed
Bubble, selection and insertion sort, traced pass by pass
Counting comparisons to see why some algorithms are faster
The software development life cycle: analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance
Planning and documenting a larger program, and working on a team project with clear roles
ICS3U exam review: tracing questions, written code and longer design questions
projects: A searchable, sortable record list built from a file, with a short design document and test log
week_15_16.practice: Trace each sort on a new list by hand, then confirm with code
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a mixed ICS3U-style review paper plus a program built from a written specification

phase_3_ics4u_toolkit.title: PHASE 3: The ICS4U Toolkit, Final Project and Exam Review (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_ics4u_toolkit.description: What we teach for Grade 12: recursion, object-oriented design, efficiency and large, fully documented programs, then the final project and exam review. ICS4U batches begin with a fast review of Phases 1 and 2.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Recursion
topics: Base case and recursive case, explained with small examples
Tracing recursion with a call stack diagram
Recursive versions of factorial, sums, string reversal and power
Recursive binary search and an introduction to merge sort
When recursion is clearer than a loop, and when it is slower
Common recursion mistakes: a missing base case and a case that never shrinks
projects: Write three recursive solutions and their loop versions, and compare them in a short written note
week_17_18.practice: Draw the call stack for every recursion question before running the code

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Classes and Object-Oriented Design
topics: Classes and objects: attributes, methods and constructors in Java and Python
Encapsulation: private data and public methods
Designing classes from a description: nouns, responsibilities and relationships
Lists of objects, and sorting objects by a chosen field
Inheritance and when to use it, with a simple class diagram
Documenting classes and methods so another programmer can use them
projects: An object-oriented library, inventory or game roster program with a class diagram and documentation
week_19_20.practice: Design the classes on paper first, then build them one method at a time with tests
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a recursion trace and a small class design, reviewed with written feedback

month_6_final_project_and_exam_review.title: Month 6: Efficiency, the Final Project and Exam Review

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Efficiency and Large Documented Programs
topics: Comparing algorithms by counting steps, with an introduction to big-O language
Choosing data structures for the job: lists, dictionaries or maps, and sets
Modular design for larger programs: files, classes and clear interfaces
Version control basics with Git so work is never lost
If your school sets a final project or culminating task: reading the brief, scoping it and planning milestones
Writing user documentation, internal comments and a test log
projects: A project plan and working first version for the student's own final project, built by the student
week_21_22.practice: Weekly milestone check-ins: what was built, what was tested, what is next

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Exam Review Technique
topics: Making a one-page summary for each topic of the school course
Tracing questions: working steadily with a trace table under time
Writing code on paper: structure first, then details, then a quick self-check
Design and explanation questions: answering exactly what is asked
Timed review papers in the style of school exams, with careful review afterwards
Reading the teacher's exam outline so revision matches what will be assessed
projects: A personal review pack: topic summaries, a mistakes list and two reviewed timed papers
week_23_24.practice: A timed mixed review each week, with every mistake written up and fixed
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: a timed review paper plus a short live walk-through of the student's own project code

faqs.question: Does this course give my child an Ontario high school credit?
faqs.answer: No. Modern Age Coders teaches alongside school and does not grant Ontario high school credits. ICS3U and ICS4U are each worth one credit, and a family who needs the credit takes the course through the student's school or a ministry-inspected credit provider. Our course helps the student understand and do well in the school course they are already taking.

faqs.question: Is ICS3U hard?
faqs.answer: It is often a student's first full programming course, so the early weeks can feel steep. The hard part is usually not the syntax but turning a problem into steps. That is why we teach problem solving and algorithm design before code, use trace tables, and practise little and often. Most of the difficulty eases once a student can plan a program before typing it.

faqs.question: Does the course use Python or Java?
faqs.answer: Whichever your school uses. Some ICS3U and ICS4U classes use Python, others use Java. We teach in the school's language so the work transfers straight back to class, and when it helps we show the same idea in the other language too.

faqs.question: What do ICS3U and ICS4U cover?
faqs.answer: The ministry describes ICS3U as a course where students "design software independently and as part of a team, using industry-standard programming tools and applying the software development life-cycle model", and ICS4U as one where students "use modular design principles to create complex and fully documented programs, according to industry standards". In each Grade 11 and 12 course the first strand is Programming Concepts and Skills, the second is Software Development, and the fourth deals with the role of computers in society. Your school's course outline gives the detail for your class.

faqs.question: Does my child need to take ICS3U before ICS4U?
faqs.answer: Yes. The ministry lists the ICS4U prerequisite as "Introduction to Computer Science, Grade 11, University Preparation", which is ICS3U. ICS3U itself has no prerequisite, so a student can start it without a Grade 10 computer course.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ICS3U and ICS3C?
faqs.answer: Both are Grade 11 computer courses and neither has a prerequisite. ICS3U is the University Preparation course, Introduction to Computer Science. ICS3C is the College Preparation course, Introduction to Computer Programming, which the ministry describes as introducing "computer programming concepts and practices". This companion course is built around ICS3U and ICS4U.

faqs.question: How does ICS3U connect to university computer science?
faqs.answer: Some programs name it directly. The University of Waterloo's Computer Science page lists "Grade 11 U Introduction to Computer Science", which is ICS3U, as a recommended course. The required courses on that page are mainly Grade 12 math and English, so a recommended course is an addition, not a replacement. Always check each university's current admission page. We make no admission promises; we help the student build real computer science understanding.

faqs.question: Will you do my child's assignments or final project?
faqs.answer: No. School work stays the student's own. We explain concepts, ask questions, review code the student has written and suggest how to improve it, and we follow the school's rules on outside help. That is also the only kind of help that lasts into the exam room.

faqs.question: Can you help with exam review?
faqs.answer: Yes. The course teaches exam technique directly: tracing code by hand, writing code on paper, answering design and explanation questions, and timed review papers with careful review afterwards. We also use the teacher's exam outline so revision matches what will actually be assessed.

faqs.question: Can my child join partway through the school year?
faqs.answer: Yes, the course is joinable any month. We start from the student's current unit and next assignment, fill gaps from earlier units as needed, and keep pace with the school course from then on. ICS4U students begin with a quick review of the ICS3U ideas they will rely on.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or 1-on-1. Weekdays or weekends, flexible: choose your batch, or for a very personalised plan choose 1-on-1 at your convenience, weekend mornings or weekdays. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher looks at where your child is in ICS3U or ICS4U, works through a short problem with them, and suggests whether group, mini batch or 1-on-1 classes fit best. There is no obligation to enrol.
